plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 9: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three mutually perpendicular planes cutting through one another, drawn as flat colored parallelograms with no coordinate axes displayed. A green plane stands roughly upright facing the viewer, labeled x = 1 in matching green at its upper right. A red plane meets it at a right angle, tilted so it reads as a tall diamond passing behind and around the green sheet, labeled y = -2 in red beneath the drawing. A blue plane lies nearly horizontal and slices through both others, labeled z = 2 in blue at its right edge. The sheets overlap so each is partly hidden by the others, giving a sectioned, interlocking block in which the visible pieces alternate in color where they cross. A small black dot near the center is labeled (1, -1, 2), which conflicts with the red plane label y = -2; as drawn, the displayed point does not satisfy all three displayed plane equations. The drawing still gives geometric meaning to a system of three linear equations in three variables, but the plane label or point label must be corrected before the marked point can be treated as the simultaneous solution.

elements: Green plane at x = 1, perpendicular to the x-axis
Red plane at y = -2 (or y = -1), perpendicular to the y-axis
Blue plane at z = 2, perpendicular to the z-axis
Black dot at the intersection of the three planes
Callout line from the black dot to its coordinate text
Coordinate text label '(1, -1, 2)'
Equation label 'x = 1' in green text
Equation label 'y = -2' (or 'y = -1') in red text
Equation label 'z = 2' in blue text

interactions.teaches: Rotating the view reveals that the three planes are mutually perpendicular, and each fixes exactly one coordinate in 3D space.
Hovering over a plane or its label highlights it, isolating its specific 2D sheet of solutions from the rest of the busy scene.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World-space is a standard 3D Cartesian system. Planes are flat squares roughly 6x6 units. Green plane is at x=1 (spans y and z). Blue plane is at z=2 (spans x and y). Red plane is at y=-2 when 'As Printed', and y=-1 when 'Corrected' (spans x and z). Colors: green #39B54A, red #ED1C24, blue #0071BC. The intersection dot is black and follows the planes' true intersection: (1,-2,2) or (1,-1,2). When 'As Printed', the red plane's label is 'y = -2', but the dot's label remains '(1, -1, 2)' to recreate the error. When 'Corrected', red label becomes 'y = -1' and matches the geometry. Ensure planes are double-sided.
interactionPlan.notes: To show the interior intersection clearly, render the planes with transparent=true, opacity=0.85, and side=THREE.DoubleSide. For the 'buildSystem' state, hide/show planes by fading their opacity. When toggling the correction, smoothly animate the red plane's position along the Y axis so the user visibly sees it shift to satisfy the coordinate.

Adjust the dimensions and center offsets of the individual planes so their visible boundaries more closely match the specific framing in the source figure.

discrepancies: The visual orientation of the red and green planes is swapped compared to the source figure (the source incorrectly drew the x=1 plane spanning the x-axis, which the code mathematically corrected, altering the visual composition)
The plane equation labels (x=1, y=-2, z=2) are missing or cropped out of the visible viewport
The planes are rendered as perfect axis-aligned rectangles, whereas the source figure uses oblique quadrilaterals that create a staggered, non-rectangular silhouette
evaluation.notes: An outstanding pedagogical implementation that correctly identifies and interactive-ly addresses a mathematical contradiction in the source figure, though it results in visually swapped planes and cropped labels.
action_items: Adjust the 3D coordinates of the plane equation labels so they remain comfortably within the visible viewport.
If strict visual parity is preferred over mathematical exactness, consider swapping the geometrical axes of the red and green planes to match the source's (flawed) drawing.
Use custom polygonal geometries rather than default PlaneGeometry to reproduce the specific slanted, jagged silhouette of the original planes.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interactivity scores are perfect, and the remaining issues are minor visual discrepancies and cropped labels that do not detract from an otherwise outstanding implementation.
